historia.title: The Iberian Sanctuary of El Pajarillo
historia.subtitle: 2,400 years ago, the Iberian aristocracy of Iltiraka claimed the wild Jandulilla valley and raised a monumental heroic sanctuary in Huelma, Jaén.

iberico_content.title: The Heroic Sanctuary of El Pajarillo (4th Century BCE)
iberico_content.body:
Strategically raised on a promontory overlooking the Jandulilla valley, the Sanctuary of El Pajarillo is one of the pinnacle monuments of Iberian protohistory (c. 350 BCE).

Conceived as a stepped ceremonial terrace across three platforms supported by ashlar stone walls, its summit hosted the heroic sculptural ensemble depicting the mythic struggle between a noble warrior and a wild beast: the monumental Wolf's Head, accompanied by protective lions and winged griffins, embodying power, valor, and aristocratic apotheosis.
iberico_content.facil: El Pajarillo is an archaeological site in Huelma. Over 2,300 years ago, the Iberians built a sacred place in memory of a hero. The stone sculptures were discovered in the fields and it is now protected by law.

iltiraka_content.title: The Territory of Iltiraka: A Valley to be Brought Under Control
iltiraka_content.body:
2,400 years ago, at the beginning of the 4th century BCE, the oppidum of Iltiraka —Úbeda la Vieja— turned its attention to this valley. It decided to claim a wild territory: the valley of the Jandulilla River.

For the Iberian people, the Jandulilla Valley was a wild territory (silva): a deep forest, the domain of wolves and fantastic beings, a place where human power had not yet reached. These were territories they sought to incorporate, and for this, a hero was needed to legitimise the process.

The oppidum of Iltiraka had a project to establish new settlements. It established another settlement at Loma del Perro (between present-day Úbeda and Jódar), controlled the routes ascending from the south and, at the headwaters of the river, built a sanctuary in memory of its founding hero: El Pajarillo. Thus, a territory under the control of a lineage (pagus) was created.
iltiraka_content.facil: 2,400 years ago, the Iberian city of Iltiraka wanted to master this wild valley. To make it their own, they honored a hero and built a sacred sanctuary: El Pajarillo.

fontanar_content.title: A Sacred Landscape: The Ritual Path & El Fontanar
fontanar_content.body:
Recent research suggests that Iltiraka did not just take the valley: it made it sacred. Beside the River Jandulilla it raised two places of worship: the sanctuary of El Pajarillo and the monument of El Fontanar —whose scene of a divine union is unique in the Iberian world—, linked by a ritual path.

To walk it was to relive the founding hero's journey to the land of the dead, and so the lineage's territory became sacred ground.
fontanar_content.facil: The Iberians connected two sacred places along the river with a ceremonial path. Walking along it remembered the hero's journey and blessed the whole valley.

timeline.title: Chronological Milestones & Archaeological Discoveries
timeline.subtitle: From Iberian colonization by Iltiraka (4th c. BCE) to the sculptural discoveries of 1933 and 1993, and excavations by the University of Jaén.

events.text: Emergence of fortified oppida in the Upper Guadalquivir (Puente Tablas) and stone lineage sculpture (Cerrillo Blanco, Porcuna).
The oppidum of Iltiraka colonizes the Jandulilla valley and erects the Heroic Sanctuary of El Pajarillo and the Wolf monument.
Crisis of clientelist aristocracies: El Pajarillo is ritually decommissioned, demolished, and abandoned.
Discovery of the first Iberian lion sculpture during construction of the road between Solera and the N-324.
Discovery of a second lion and a headless figure with falcata during farming work. Emergency excavations by the University of Jaén.
Official decree declaring the Cortijo del Pajarillo site an Asset of Cultural Interest (BIC) as an Archaeological Zone.
